food.text: The Mumun pottery period, dated to approximately 1500 to 300 BC, is known for the origins of intensive agriculture and complex societies. This happened on both the Korean Peninsula and the Japanese archipelago.

Mumun farmers did not live on rice alone. They grew millets, barley, wheat and legumes, and they continued to hunt and fish. Although rice was grown in the Early and Middle Mumun, it was not the dominant crop.

Before the Mumun, the people of the Jeulmun period lived by hunting, gathering, foraging and small-scale cultivation of wild plants. It was during the Jeulmun that the cultivation of millet and rice reached the Korean Peninsula from the Asian continent.
Rice agriculture appears in Early Mumun, added to the earlier millet farming. This was the start of the Korean Peninsula's move toward the rice-growing that later became central to its food.
Mumun culture is the beginning of a long-term tradition of rice-farming in Korea. That tradition links Mumun culture with the present day.

Archaeologists estimate the adzuki bean was domesticated around 3000 BC, after wild adzuki spread naturally to central China and Japan. Yet adzuki beans and soybeans dating from 3000 BC to 2000 BC are still largely within the wild size range. Enlarged seeds came later, in periods with plough use.
Early Mumun farmers harvested with stone knives, in particular lunate and bay-shaped ones. These knives appear in the same period as the first rice agriculture alongside millet farming.

art.text: The earliest examples of Korean art date to around 3000 BC, in the Stone Age. They mainly consist of votive sculptures and petroglyphs, which were more recently rediscovered.
Jeulmun, or Comb-pattern, pottery is found in Korea after 7000 BC. Vessels with comb-patterns over their whole surface are concentrated at sites in west-central Korea between 3500 and 2000 BC.

Between 2000 BC and 300 BC, bronze items began to be imported and made in Korea. They included weapons such as swords, daggers and spearheads, plus ritual mirrors, bells and rattles. These items were buried in dolmens with the cultural elite, in burials that also held comma-shaped kokkok beads of nephrite.
The Mumun period takes its name from the Korean word for undecorated or plain cooking and storage vessels. These plain pots make up a large part of the pottery found across the whole period.

The best-known dogū type is the Shakōkidogū, or 'goggle-eyed dogū,' named for eyes resembling snow goggles. It features exaggerated female buttocks, chest and thighs, with an abdomen covered in patterns that seem to have been painted with vermilion. Unbroken figures are rare: most are missing an arm, leg or other body part, and in many cases the parts have been cut off.

The Hollow Dogū is a clay figurine from Japan's Late Jōmon period, dated to around 1500 to 1300 BC. A housewife turning over the soil with a hoe to harvest potatoes unearthed it in August 1975 at what became the Chobonaino Site in Hakodate, Hokkaido, near a Late Jōmon pit burial. One theory proposes it was used in a funeral ritual, with the liquid-filled figure tipped up by the officiant and its contents poured over the body of the deceased and into the open mouths of the celebrants. It is one of five dogū designated National Treasures.

literature.text: Old Chosŏn, Korea's first kingdom, was said to have been founded in 2333 BCE by Tan'gun, believed to be the son of the heavenly prince Hwanung and a bear-woman named Ungnyeo. Though a mythological figure, Tan'gun's legend has played an important role in shaping Korean identity.
Tan'gun is remembered as the grandson of heaven and son of a bear who founded Korea's first kingdom in 2333 BC. His descendants are traditionally said to carry the surname Park or Pai.

Korea preserves many separate founding myths for its early kingdoms, but the tale of legendary king Dangun founding the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon, is treated differently. It has become the founding myth of the entire Korean nation, rather than of just one early state.

The earliest known written version of the Tan'gun legend appears only in the 13th-century Samguk yusa, which claims to cite an older, now-lost Korean record called Gogi as well as China's Book of Wei. However, no mention of Tan'gun actually survives in today's version of the Book of Wei.

In the legend, Hwanung, Tan'gun's father, descended to a mountain called Taebaeksan with 3,000 followers and founded a settlement named Sinsi, or City of God. There, with ministers of clouds, rain, and wind, he taught early humans various arts, medicine, and agriculture.

While Hwanung is credited with teaching early humans agriculture and medicine, Korean legend separately attributes the invention of acupuncture and moxibustion to his son, Tan'gun. This detail appears alongside the broader account of Tan'gun founding Gojoseon around 2333 BC.

Accounts disagree on exactly when Tan'gun ascended the throne during the reign of the legendary Chinese Emperor Yao. The Samguk yusa places it in Yao's 50th year, the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty in his first year, and the Tongguk t'onggam in his 25th year.
Tan'gun, remembered for founding Gojoseon around 2333 BC, has an unusual linguistic legacy. Many Korean historians regard his name as etymologically identical to Tengri.

science.text: Farmers of the Mumun Period began using multiple cropping systems some time after 1500 BC. This advance in food production altered how Mumun communities fed themselves and hastened the start of intensive agriculture on the Korean Peninsula.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Korean pottery makers decorated whole vessels with comb patterns, and such Jeulmun pottery is concentrated at sites in west-central Korea between 3500 and 2000 BC. Settlements such as Amsa-dong and Chitam-ni existed at that time.

Korea and adjacent areas of East Asia seem to have been part of the domestication region of the soybean between 1500 and 500 BC. Paddy-field wet-rice cultivation was also introduced into the southern peninsula around this time.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Korea

science.text: Korean archaeologists traditionally, until the 1990s, dated the start of the Bronze Age to 1500 or 1000 BC. Yet bronze technology was not adopted in southern Korea until about 700 BC, so the dating has long been debated.

politics.text: Old Chosŏn, also known as Gojoseon, was the first kingdom on the Korean Peninsula, traditionally said to have been founded in 2333 BCE by the legendary king Tan'gun. It reportedly possessed the most advanced culture on the peninsula at the time, marking a step toward the more centralized states of later Korean history.

According to legend, Tan'gun—called the 'grandson of heaven' and 'son of a bear'—was born to the heavenly prince Hwanung and a bear-woman named Ungnyeo. He is said to have founded Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, in 2333 BC.

Korea's dolmens, the most concentrated in the world, were used to mark the graves of the ruling elite and are linked to the Neolithic and Bronze Age cultures of Korea. Some even depict astronomical formations dated as early as 3000 BC.
politics.source_title: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites

politics.text: The Gojoseon kingdom, Korea's first, was traditionally founded in northern Korea and southern Manchuria in 2333 BC. Its earliest written historical record appears in the ancient Chinese text Guanzi.

The 13th-century Samguk Yusa records that Gojoseon was founded in the year of gyeongin, corresponding to 2311 BC, fifty years after the enthronement of the legendary Chinese Emperor Yao. Its author, Il-yeon, added that he personally believed the true founding date was the year of jeongsa, or 2284 BC.

Unlike the widely cited 2333 BCE date, North Korea officially dates Tan'gun's founding of Gojoseon to the early 30th century BC. This reflects a divergent modern claim about the antiquity of Korea's first kingdom.

Citing Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian and Yi Sŭnghyu's Chewang un'gi, the later chronicle Tongguk t'onggam rejected the Samguk Yusa's dating. It instead argued that Gojoseon was founded in the year of mujin, corresponding to 2333 BC, only twenty-five years after the rise of Emperor Yao.

philosophy.text: During the later part of Japan's Jōmon period, people made small clay dogū figurines. Some scholars theorize they acted as effigies of people, working as a kind of sympathetic magic: illness or any other misfortune may have been thought to transfer into the dogū, which was then destroyed to clear it away. Most dogū have marks on the face, chest and shoulders that suggest tattooing and probable incision with bamboo.
Some dolmens on the Korean Peninsula depict astronomical formations dated to around 3000 BC. The reason for these markings remains unknown.
philosophy.source_title: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites

philosophy.text: The Samguk yusa says Tan'gun was born to the heavenly prince Hwanung and a bear-woman named Ungnyeo. He is credited with establishing Gojoseon in 2333 BCE.
According to the Samguk yusa's account, the Gojoseon kingdom was founded around 2333 BC. Its territory is described as spanning both northern Korea and southern Manchuria.
Chinese sources say that in the 12th century BCE, after Gojoseon's founding, the sage Jizi, also known as Kija, migrated into the region. He was a member of the royal family of the Shang dynasty.

Ancient Korean sources disagree on exactly when Tan'gun took the throne. The Samguk yusa places it in the 50th year of the legendary Chinese Emperor Yao's reign, the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty says the first year, and the Tongguk t'onggam says the 25th year.

The monk Il-yeon, who recorded the Tan'gun legend in the Samguk yusa, is best known for citing 2311 BC, the year of gyeongin, as Gojoseon's founding year. Yet he also noted he personally believed the true founding date might have been 2284 BC, the year of jeongsa.

culture.text: According to the Samguk yusa, written in 1281, the kingdom of Gojoseon was founded in 2333 BC by Dangun, said to be descended from heaven. No evidence supports the legend, yet it has played an important role in developing Korean national identity.

Between 3500 and 2000 BC, pottery decorated with comb patterns over the whole vessel was concentrated at sites in west-central Korea. This Jeulmun pottery marks a time when settlements such as Amsa-dong and Chitam-ni existed.
The direct ancestors of the present Korean people are thought to be the Neolithic people of about 2000 BC. The earlier Paleolithic people are likely not their direct ancestors.

Jeulmun pottery bears basic design and form similarities to pottery of the Russian Maritime Province, Mongolia, the Amur and Sungari River basins of Manchuria, the Baiyue of southeastern China and the Jōmon culture in Japan. Its style hints at wide contacts across the region.

Korea's Bronze Age is often held to have begun around 900 to 800 BC, but the transition may have started as far back as 2300 BC. Bronze daggers, mirrors, jewelry and weaponry have been found, along with evidence of walled-town polities.

In the Middle Jōmon period (3000-2000 BCE), simple decorations made with cord or scratching gave way to highly elaborate designs. Among the most distinctive forms are the so-called flame vessels and the closely related crown-formed vessels.

It has been conjectured that climate changes around 2000 BCE triggered a rapid migration eastward into Korea, as well as westward and southward. The movement supposedly took just five to six generations and spread the same metal working technology, and in places horse riding, across some 4,000 miles.
